items.label: text
items.text: The reason that we keep stressing the use of inert electrodes is that what the electrode is made of can sometimes affect the products you get. items.label: text
items.text: Cl-(aq) and OH-(aq) are both attracted by the positive anode. It is slightly easier to remove electrons from (oxidise) the hydroxide ion than from the chloride ion, but there isn't much difference. There are, however, many, many more chloride ions present in the solution, and so it is mainly these that are oxidised at the anode:

items.label: formula
items.text: 2 C | ( a q ) \rightarrow C | _ { 2 } ( g ) + 2 e ^ { - }

items.label: text
items.text: If the electrolysis is carried on for a long time, we can work out what the final solution remaining at the end will be. The ions in the solution were:

items.label: text
items.text: from NaCl: Na^+ CK

items.label: text
items.text: from H2O: OH-

items.label: text
items.text: Cl- and H+ ions were removed from the solution by being discharged at the electrodes, so we are left with Na+ and OH-, sodium hydroxide solution.

items.label: section_header
items.text: THE ELECTROLYSIS OF COPPER(II) SULFATE SOLUTION USING INERT ELECTRODES

items.label: text
items.text: The copper(ll) ions and hydrogen ions (from the water) will be attracted to the cathode. Copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series, which means that it is easier to add electrons to copper ions to form an atom. The cathode will get coated with pink-brown copper:

items.label: formula
items.text: C u ^ { 2 + ( a q ) + 2 e - } \rightarrow C u ( s ) \quad \text {reduction}

items.label: text
items.text: Sulfate ions and hydroxide ions (from the water) will be attracted to the anode. Sulfate ions aren't easy to oxidise. Instead, you get oxygen from the oxidation of hydroxide ions from the water:

items.label: formula
items.text: 4 O H ( a q ) \to 2 H _ { 2 } O ( 1 ) + O _ { 2 } ( g ) + 4 e ^ { - } \quad \text {exidition}

items.text: If the electrolysis is continued for a long time the copper(ll) ions will eventually all be used up, and so the colour of the solution will fade from blue to colourless. What is left in the solution? The ions originally present were:

items.label: text
items.text: from CuSO4: CU2 SO{42

items.label: text
items.text: from water: H+ OH

items.label: text
items.text: Copper ions and hydroxide ions are discharged at the electrodes. Hydrogen ions from the water aren't being discharged and neither are the sulfate ions. The solution turns into dilute sulfuric acid (H2SO). The electrolysis will then continue as for dilute sulfuric acid (see below).
